AL.stateParks: Alabama's segment is short (Perdido Key/Orange Beach to the MS line) but Gulf State Park (Gulf Shores) and Meaher State Park (Spanish Fort, on Mobile Bay) sit essentially on route. Primitive/tent sites vary by park and season — roughly $15-30/night — and every reservation adds a $5.25 (some parks $5.00) non-refundable reservation fee plus a ~4-4.25% nightly 'resort fee'. Reservations run through ReserveAlabama (reserve.alapark.com, 1-800-ALAPARK); walk-ups are accepted when sites are open. Camping includes entry; some parks charge day-users a small gate fee.
AL.cityParks: No city-park camping tradition here — coastal AL municipal parks generally close at dusk by local ordinance and overnight camping is banned unless posted otherwise. With only 1-2 nights in the state and Gulf SP/Meaher SP on route, cyclists rarely need to ask. If stuck near Mobile, call the police non-emergency line rather than stealth-camping in a beach town.
AL.restAreas: Alabama prohibits overnight parking AND camping at its rest areas/welcome centers — the strictest of the Gulf states. The I-10 welcome centers are irrelevant to the bike route anyway. Do not plan any AL rest-area overnight.
AL.publicLands: Effectively zero federal dispersed-camping land on the corridor — no BLM, and Conecuh NF is far north of the route. The Gulf beaches are state/city controlled with camping bans. Treat AL as a paid-campground/Warmshowers state.
AL.notes: Gulf State Park is a resort-priced park (improved sites can run $40-60); its primitive loop is the budget play. Book the Gulf Shores area ahead — snowbird season is ramping up by late September. The AL crossing is 2 days max, so one reservation covers it.

MS.stateParks: The route hugs the coast ~80 mi (Pascagoula-Ocean Springs-Bay St. Louis-Pearlington); Shepard State Park (Gautier) and Buccaneer State Park (Waveland) are both essentially on route. Buccaneer reservable tent sites run ~$28/night; its first-come primitive area is ~$18-20/night. MS state parks reserve through ReserveAmerica (mississippistateparks.reserveamerica.com); walk-up is fine for primitive loops on weekdays. Small per-vehicle day-use fees exist but camping covers entry.
MS.cityParks: Overnight camping in municipal parks is banned by default on the developed Gulf Coast — these are casino/beach towns, not the small-town-hospitality belt. The ask-city-hall tradition doesn't really operate here. With two well-placed state parks, the coast is easy to cover legally.
MS.restAreas: MDOT allows overnight PARKING but no camping — vehicles parked over ~8 continuous hours are considered long-term and can be removed by MDOT or Highway Patrol, and 'recreational camping' (tents, gear out) is explicitly disallowed. Not usable for a cyclist with a tent.
MS.publicLands: De Soto National Forest (free dispersed camping, 14-day limit) lies ~20-30 miles north of the coastal route — the corridor does not touch it, and detouring costs a day. Coastal land is state/private. Skip it unless rerouting inland.
MS.notes: Buccaneer SP in Waveland is the classic pre-New Orleans overnight (day's ride to the city). Fall is shoulder season on the coast — sites are gettable, but check tropical-weather closures; these low-lying parks shut for storms. MDWFP phone numbers answer fee questions faster than the website.

LA.stateParks: Unimproved (no-hookup) sites run $18-27/night + tax, improved $28-42; a $4.50 non-refundable reservation fee applies to every booking including walk-ins, and there's a $3/person day-use fee for non-campers. Reservations via lastateparks.com / 1-833-609-0686, and the system explicitly welcomes walk-ups when sites are open. On or near route: Fontainebleau and Fairview-Riverside (Mandeville, north shore) and Bayou Segnette (Westwego, across from New Orleans); Lake Fausse Pointe sits near the New Iberia stretch.
LA.cityParks: This is where the ask-the-town tradition begins: Cajun-country towns (Donaldsonville-Morgan City-Eunice-Kinder-DeRidder-Merryville belt) have a history of letting touring cyclists pitch in town parks or under pavilions with permission. Default law is still no-overnight-camping in municipal parks unless posted or permitted — so call city hall before 4:30pm or the police non-emergency line, get a name, set up late, leave early. ACA map panels mark several cyclist-tolerant town parks in this stretch.
LA.restAreas: Louisiana has no statewide overnight statute, but the practical rule is no overnight parking or camping at rest areas — several I-10 facilities post limits or close overnight, and tents are out everywhere. Don't build LA rest areas into the plan.
LA.publicLands: Kisatchie NF is far north of the corridor — not reachable. The real LA public-land option is Wildlife Management Areas: camping is free of nightly fees but ONLY in designated areas, max 16 consecutive days per 30 (then 48 hours out), and you need a WMA Access Permit (included with LA hunting/fishing licenses, free under 18) plus a WMA Camping Permit per party at LDWF campgrounds; a Self-Clearing Permit covers most other WMA activities. Check which WMAs sit near the route (e.g., Atchafalaya-basin areas) before counting on one.
LA.notes: Buying the cheapest LDWF license/stamp that carries WMA access is the legal key to free WMA camping — sort it online before arriving. October-January is gun season on WMAs: designated camp areas fill with hunters and blaze orange is essential. New Orleans itself = Warmshowers or hostel territory; there is no legal cheap camping in the city.

TX.stateParks: Texas is the only state on the route that stacks a per-person daily ENTRANCE fee ($3-8/person/day, e.g. $4 at Seminole Canyon) on top of the site fee — and it's charged for every day you're in the park. Tent/primitive sites run $10-15 (Seminole Canyon: primitive $10, water sites $15), electric $20-25. Reservations through the Texas State Parks Reservation System (tpwd.texas.gov, 512-389-8900), 5-month rolling window; walk-ups get unreserved sites. The $70 State Parks Pass kills all entrance fees — only worth it if you'll log ~10+ park-days crossing the state.
TX.cityParks: Texas is the heart of the Southern Tier city-park tradition: many small West/South Texas towns officially or informally let cyclists camp in the city park — some post it, some run $5-10 honor boxes, most just expect you to check in at city hall (before close) or the police/sheriff non-emergency line. Legally, overnight camping in a municipal park is prohibited unless the town allows it, so the phone call IS the legal cover; get the officer's or clerk's name. This works far better in 1,000-person towns than in cities.
TX.restAreas: TxDOT allows a 24-hour stay at rest areas, picnic areas, and travel information centers — but Transp. Code 545.411 makes erecting a tent, shelter, or structure an offense, and sleeping must happen inside a vehicle. Cyclists do quietly overnight at remote West Texas picnic areas (there's no vehicle to sleep in), but know it's technically illegal — cowboy-camp without the tent, arrive at dusk, leave at dawn, and have a fallback.
TX.publicLands: Texas is ~95% private land — essentially no BLM or National Forest anywhere near the corridor, and fences run to the highway shoulder. The one federal bright spot is Amistad National Recreation Area at Del Rio (NPS): cheap primitive first-come campgrounds right off the route. Otherwise the TX toolkit is state parks (Seminole Canyon, Davis Mountains-area), city parks, and RV parks that take tents.
TX.notes: Budget for the entrance-fee stacking — a $10 primitive site is really $14-18/night solo. West of Del Rio the gaps get serious (Comstock-Sanderson-Marathon); the sheriff check-in habit doubles as a safety net out there. Never camp on roadside land that isn't a signed public facility — trespassing on Texas ranchland is taken seriously.

NM.stateParks: Since Jan 1, 2025: primitive camping $10/night residents / $15 non-residents, developed sites $15/$20, hookups extra ($10 electric, $5 water/sewer) — fees are per vehicle per day and explicitly include walk-in and BICYCLE campers. Reservations via ReserveAmerica (newmexicostateparks.reserveamerica.com, 1-877-664-7787), $3.50/night reservation fee capped at $10; first-come sites remain at most parks. On route: Leasburg Dam (near Las Cruces), then Percha Dam and Caballo Lake SPs right on the approach to Hillsboro/Emory Pass, and City of Rocks SP between Silver City and Deming.
NM.cityParks: Less of an institution than Texas, but the same ask-first protocol works in villages like Hatch and Hillsboro — default ordinance position is no overnight in town parks without permission. Small-town NM is generally cyclist-tolerant on this corridor since the ACA route is known. Police non-emergency or village office before 5pm.
NM.restAreas: NMDOT rest areas allow up to 24 hours and overnight parking, but no camping and no sleeping outside a vehicle — so no tents. Same practical situation as Texas: not a legal tent option for a cyclist.
NM.publicLands: The best public-land stretch on the whole route: BLM land around Las Cruces (Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks NM area) allows free dispersed camping, and the Gila National Forest over Emory Pass (NM-152, Black Range) allows free dispersed camping forest-wide — 14-day limit per 30 days, camp 100 ft from water, existing fire rings, no permit needed. Iron Creek Campground and other NFS sites sit right on the Emory Pass climb.
NM.notes: Non-resident pricing means a solo cyclist pays $15 even for primitive state-park sites — Gila NF dispersed camping is free and directly on route, so use it over Emory Pass. Nights above 7,000 ft in late October are below freezing; Emory Pass tops at 8,228 ft. Fall gun deer seasons run in the Gila — orange on the tent.

AZ.stateParks: AZ State Parks camping runs $25-50/night (tent/non-hookup sites typically at the low end), plus a $3.60 non-refundable reservation fee; book at azstateparks.com up to 13 months out, walk-ups OK when open. Fees rose Feb 25, 2025, and the all-parks annual pass jumped to $200 — irrelevant for a pass-through cyclist. On route: Roper Lake SP (Safford) and Lost Dutchman SP (Apache Junction); note some AZ parks also charge per-vehicle day-use that camping covers.
AZ.cityParks: Arizona towns generally ban camping in municipal parks and, post-Grants Pass (2024), metro-Phoenix-area ordinances are actively enforced — do not try it in the Valley. Small towns on the eastern segment (Duncan, Pima) have been known to host cyclists at town parks with a call ahead — Duncan in particular has cyclist lore — but always ask city hall/marshal first. Outside towns, public land is so abundant that city parks matter less here.
AZ.restAreas: ADOT rest areas permit overnight parking with no posted maximum, but camping (tents, gear outside a vehicle) is prohibited. Same story: fine for motorists, not a tent option.
AZ.publicLands: Excellent: Coronado NF near Safford, then Tonto NF from Globe through Superior toward Apache Junction (free dispersed camping, 14-day/30 limit; free first-come Oak Flat CG area near Superior sits close to US 60), and wide-open BLM in the west (Harquahala/Ranegras plains around Salome-Hope-Brenda; La Posa LTVA at Quartzsite is near the I-10 corridor). Standard BLM dispersed rules: free, 14 days per 28 within 25 miles, use existing sites. Also note AZ State Trust Land checkerboards much of the desert — that requires its own permit.
AZ.notes: Arizona State Trust land (unfenced desert that looks like BLM) legally requires a $15/year individual recreation permit (14 camping nights/yr, buy online at land.az.gov) — either buy one or verify you're on true BLM before pitching. Metro Phoenix is a 2-day no-camping gauntlet: plan Warmshowers/motel for Apache Junction-Tempe-Wickenburg. Check Tonto NF fire restrictions — fall can still be stage 1/2.

CA.stateParks: The budget crown jewel: coastal CA state parks offer first-come, first-served hike/bike sites at a per-person fee — currently $10-15/person/night (San Elijo SB charges $15), no reservation possible or needed, 1-2 night max (San Elijo: 2 nights, 10 days/yr). On the San Diego→LA leg that means San Elijo SB, South Carlsbad SB, San Onofre/San Mateo, Doheny SB, and Crystal Cove — arrive by mid-afternoon. Standard reservable sites (ReserveCalifornia) run $35-60+ on this coast, so hike/bike is the play. The desert segment (Blythe→Jacumba) has no state parks on route.
CA.cityParks: Do not attempt city-park camping in Southern California — municipal anti-camping ordinances are aggressively enforced in San Diego, Orange County, and LA, and the small-town-hospitality tradition does not exist here. The hike/bike network exists precisely so cyclists don't need it. In the Imperial Valley towns (Brawley, El Centro), use motels or nearby BLM instead.
CA.restAreas: Caltrans: 8-hour maximum stay per rest area per 24 hours, no camping, no tents, must be inside a vehicle — sleeping on a bench or the ground counts as camping (21 CCR 2205). Also explicitly no parking at rest areas while off biking. Zero utility for a touring cyclist.
CA.publicLands: The desert third is nearly all BLM: free 14-day dispersed camping around Palo Verde, the Imperial Sand Dunes area (Glamis), and the Yuha Desert; plus seven Long-Term Visitor Areas including Hot Spring LTVA near Holtville (right off the route, with an actual hot tub-spring). Then the Cleveland NF (Pine Valley/Descanso district): dispersed 'remote camping' requires a free permit emailed to the district ~2 days ahead, wood/charcoal fires are banned outside developed sites, and Boulder Oaks CG (recreation.gov) sits on old US-80 on route.
CA.notes: LTVA season runs Sept 15-Apr 15: inside LTVA boundaries you need a permit ($40/any 14 days, $180 season), but ordinary BLM outside LTVAs stays free — for one-night stops, camp outside the LTVA line or pay the $40 if you want the Holtville hot spring + trash service. Get the Descanso district remote-camping permit before leaving El Centro if you want to disperse in the Laguna/Pine Valley mountains. After San Diego, budget = hike/bike sites the whole way to LA.

programs.warmshowers: Warmshowers.org is the reciprocal hospitality network of touring cyclists hosting touring cyclists (bed or yard, shower, often dinner) — free to stay, with a one-time ~$30 signup contribution for new members; the website is free to use after that, while the mobile app charges cyclists a separate subscription (~$2.99/mo or $17.99/yr) unless used in host-only mode. Send personalized requests ~3-7 days ahead with a check-in message the day before; same-day requests work sometimes but are poor etiquette. Density on the Southern Tier is good in and around cities (New Orleans, Lafayette, Austin-adjacent, El Paso, Las Cruces, Silver City, Tucson/Phoenix, San Diego) and thin-to-absent across west Texas and the desert gaps — plan hosts for the expensive metros, camping for the empty stretches.
programs.churches: The ACA Southern Tier maps mark churches that have historically welcomed cyclists (lawn camping, sometimes a hall floor and shower), concentrated in the Bible-belt half — Louisiana through west Texas — and mostly Baptist and Methodist congregations in small towns. The norm: call the church office mid-afternoon (or knock), ask for the pastor or secretary, say you're a touring cyclist on the Adventure Cycling route and ask if you may pitch a tent on their grounds for one night; offer a donation and leave the site spotless. Unannounced Sunday-evening arrivals are the one timing that reliably works without a call, since people are on site.
programs.fireStations: The small-town check-in is a real institution on rural US bike routes: stop at the fire station, city hall, or sheriff's office in the late afternoon, explain you're a cross-country cyclist, and ask where they'd like you to camp — the answer is usually the city park, the fairgrounds, behind the station, or a churchyard, and the check-in itself is your legal cover plus insurance against a 2am flashlight wake-up. Volunteer fire stations in Texas and Louisiana sometimes offer water, a hose shower, or a bay floor. Always get the name of whoever said yes, arrive/settle before dark, and be gone by 7-8am.
programs.adventureCycling: Adventure Cycling's Southern Tier map set (paper + Bicycle Route Navigator app) lists campgrounds, city parks that allow camping, cyclist-friendly churches, hostels, and full service directories per map panel; the free online Route Updates & Corrections (addenda) pages carry current closures, rerouting, and camping changes reported by riders, and the Route Feedback Form feeds them. ACA's forums and the route resources pages also carry section-by-section riding-conditions notes (terrain, service gaps, water warnings). Cross-check any pre-2024 addenda against the current map edition since the route was revised.
programs.apps: For this corridor: iOverlander (free, community-sourced) is the strongest in the desert West — wild spots, water spigots, and 'asked-permission' town spots with recent check-ins; freecampsites.net (free website) is best for finding legal free options like TX picnic areas, city parks, and BLM pull-offs east of the Rockies; The Dyrt's free tier is the biggest campground database and fine for looking up state-park loops; Campendium is useful for BLM/LTVA and rest-area reviews though more features have moved behind Roadpass paywalls. Practical combo: iOverlander + freecampsites.net, both cached offline before the west-Texas and desert segments.

generalTips: Sunset math: by late October you'll lose light by 5:15-5:45pm (Mountain/Pacific) — plan to be AT camp by 4:30, which also matches the city-hall/sheriff check-in window (offices close 4:30-5:00).

Texas fee stacking is the hidden cost: a $10 primitive site + $4-8/person entrance fee makes state parks $14-18/night solo — count your planned TX park nights before buying the $70 annual pass (breakeven ~10-14 park-days for one person).

Buy the cheap legal permits before you need them: an LDWF license/permit with WMA access (free designated-area camping in Louisiana) and the $15/yr Arizona State Trust Land recreation permit — both purchasable online, both turn 'trespassing' into 'legal free camping'.

Free camping center of gravity: from Las Cruces westward, default to BLM and National Forest dispersed camping (free, 14-day limits, no permit except Cleveland NF's Descanso district, which needs a free emailed permit ~2 days ahead) and save paid sites for towns.

You arrive in LTVA country (Quartzsite/Blythe/Holtville) after the Sept 15 season opens: camp on regular BLM just OUTSIDE the LTVA boundaries for free, or pay $40 for any-14-days if you want the Hot Spring LTVA's spring, trash, and company.

October-November is gun deer season in every state you cross — on WMAs and National Forests wear blaze orange while riding and drape something orange on the tent, and avoid camping near feeders, food plots, or at dawn shooting light.

Rest areas are a vehicle-sleeper's game, not a tent camper's: every state on this route bans tents at rest areas (CA even caps stays at 8 hours), so treat TX/NM picnic-area overnights as no-tent, dusk-to-dawn, fallback-only moves.

Water is the desert budget item that isn't money: 100+ mile gaps in west Texas (Comstock-Sanderson-Marathon) and the AZ/CA desert demand 6-10L capacity; use iOverlander water POIs, and cemeteries, churches, and fire stations reliably have spigots.
Spend your Warmshowers requests on the expensive metros — New Orleans, El Paso, Phoenix, San Diego — where legal camping is nonexistent and motels are $100+; camp the cheap rural stretches instead.

After San Diego, the coastal hike/bike system ($10-15/person, first-come, no reservations possible) is your entire San Diego→LA lodging plan: San Elijo, South Carlsbad, San Onofre, Doheny, Crystal Cove — roll in by 2-3pm, respect the 1-2 night max.
